newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seen proposing rise in energy taxes.
newsitem.headline: EU seen proposing rise in energy taxes.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to adopt a plan next week to increase taxes on petrol and diesel fuel, a move many see as an attempt to introduce a tax on carbon dioxide emissions by the back door.
The proposal for a European Union directive on taxation of energy products would increase EU-wide minimum excise duties on motor and heating fuels.
It would also impose a minimum tax on electricity, natural gas and coal which are not currently covered by EU rules.
But for most products the minimum levels would be below the actual rates currently levied in the 15-nation bloc.

Like an old plan to create a European tax on CO2 emissions, the new proposal has run into fierce opposition from the European oil industry as well as major energy-intensive sectors such as the steel, cement and chemical industries.
"Our position is that such a directive should not exist," said Claude Culem, head of the economics and statistics department of the European Chemical Industry Council (CEFIC).
The industry says that the plan opens the way for a further rise in energy taxes in Europe, which are already a third higher than in the United States.

"This is not compatible with the prime goal of competitiveness, unless energy sources for industrial use are exempted, or, at the very least, that tax rates are aligned to the lowest levels charged by our major competitors outside Europe," a group of European associations in the car, chemicals, cement, steel and other sectors said in a recent statement.
The Commission's plan is largely motivated by its belief that different tax levels are distorting competition in the bloc's border-free single market.
It is also acting on a request from EU heads of government to build up existing excise duties following their failure to agree on a CO2 tax to protect the environment.

The proposal currently on the table, prepared by Internal Market and Taxation Commissioner Mario Monti, sets a minimum tax of 450 ecus ($529) per 1,000 litres of petrol from January 1, 1998. This would rise to 500 ecus in 2000 and 557 ecus in 2002.
The draft requires EU states to apply a higher tax for leaded petrol than unleaded without saying what the gap should be.

The current minimum EU rate for leaded petrol is 337 ecus and 287 for unleaded but at the end of 1996, the actual rates for unleaded petrol were all above 350 ecus, with the German, French, Belgian, Finnish and Dutch levels standing above 500 ecus. The situation was broadly the same for leaded petrol.

For diesel, the Commission is proposing a minimum rate of 343 ecus in 1998 to rise to 450 ecus in 2002 from a present 245. The actual national levels vary from 244 ecus in Greece, the lowest rate, to 436 ecus in Britain, were it is the highest.

Natural gas used as motor fuel would be taxed a minimum 3.5 ecus per gigajoule in 1998 and 6.0 ecus in 2002. The Commission also proposes to tax electricity at 1.0 ecu per megawatt/hour in 1998 and 3.0 ecus in 2002. There are currently no minimum rates for the two products.
